qs.q: Coordination is the essence of management.
o: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

Every organisation should be fully centralised

qs.q: Planning may not work in a dynamic environment.
o: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

o: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).

qs.q: Explain any three points of importance of staffing.
qs.model:
(i) Obtaining competent personnel: it helps discover and obtain competent people.

(ii) Higher performance: the right person in the right job performs better.

(iii) Optimum utilisation of human resources: it prevents over-manning and under-manning.

qs.q: Explain any three points of importance of directing.
qs.model:
(i) Initiates action: people start working towards goals.

(ii) Means of motivation: employees are inspired to give their best.

(iii) Facilitates implementation of changes: communication and leadership reduce resistance.

qs.q: Identify three factors affecting the working capital requirement of Frosty Delights and state whether each increases or decreases it.
qs.passage: Frosty Delights makes ice cream. It buys large stocks of milk and sugar from February for the summer rush, and its sales triple from April to June. It sells to big retailers on 60 days' credit, but its own suppliers demand cash.

points.p: Seasonal factors: summer peak → higher working capital
Credit allowed: 60 days to retailers → higher working capital
Credit availed: suppliers demand cash → higher working capital

qs.model:
(i) Seasonal factors: stocks are built up for the summer rush, so more working capital is needed in peak season.

(ii) Credit allowed: selling on 60 days' credit blocks funds in debtors, increasing working capital.

(iii) Credit availed: no credit from suppliers (cash purchases) increases working capital needs.
qs.hint: Summer rush; 60 days to retailers; cash to suppliers.
qs.ans: Seasonal factors, credit allowed, credit availed

qs.q: Who can file a complaint under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019? (any three)
qs.model: (i) A consumer. (ii) A registered voluntary consumer association. (iii) The Central or State Government, or the CCPA. (Also: consumers on behalf of many with the same interest; legal heir of a deceased consumer; parent or guardian of a minor.)
qs.hint: Consumer, association, government, CCPA, heir, guardian.

qs.cn: Assistance in planning and policy formulation
qs.q: Identify and explain two points of importance of business environment highlighted in the case.
qs.passage:
After the Union Budget announced lower GST on small two-wheelers and a new scheme for rural roads, the board of Pathik Motors met. Using this analysis, they decided to open 200 rural dealerships next year and design a cheaper, sturdier scooter for village roads.

Their CFO, Mr. Arvind Kulkarni, also arranged a low-interest loan under a new government scheme for manufacturers to fund the new plant.

points.p: Assistance in planning and policy formulation named
Explained + linked: analysis led to plans for 200 rural dealerships and a new scooter
Explained + linked: the firm obtained finance (low-interest loan) from its environment

qs.model:
(i) Assistance in planning and policy formulation: environmental analysis gives the basis for future plans. After studying the budget, Pathik Motors decided to “open 200 rural dealerships” and design a scooter for village roads.

(ii) Tapping useful resources: a firm obtains finance, machines, materials and labour from its environment. The CFO “arranged a low-interest loan under a new government scheme” to fund the plant.
qs.hint: What did the board decide using the analysis? What did the CFO get?
qs.ans: Assistance in planning and policy formulation; tapping useful resources

qs.q: Identify four factors that will affect the price of Cureline's medicine.
qs.passage: Cureline Pharma launched a new diabetes medicine. Its cost of production is ₹6 per tablet. The government's price authority has capped such medicines at ₹12 per tablet. Three rivals sell similar tablets at ₹10. Cureline also wants to capture a large share of the market quickly.

points.p: Product cost: ₹6 per tablet (price must cover it)

qs.model:
(i) Product cost: price should cover the cost of ₹6 per tablet.

(ii) Government and legal regulations: the price cannot exceed the ₹12 cap.

(iii) Extent of competition: rivals sell at ₹10, which limits the price.

(iv) Pricing objectives: to capture market share quickly, a lower price may be set.
qs.hint: ₹6 cost; ₹12 cap; rivals at ₹10; market share.
qs.ans: Product cost, government regulations, extent of competition, pricing objectives

qs.q: State four reliefs the Commission may order in Rahul's favour or against GlowNow.
qs.passage: GlowNow advertised that its cream 'removes all pimples in 3 days, guaranteed'. Rahul used it for a month; his skin got worse and he spent ₹15,000 on a doctor. The District Commission found the claim false.

points.p: Corrective advertisement to neutralise the false claim
Discontinue the unfair trade practice / punitive damages

qs.model:
(i) Refund of the price of the cream.

(ii) Compensation for the injury and the ₹15,000 spent on treatment.

(iii) Corrective advertisement to neutralise the misleading claim.

(iv) Discontinue the unfair trade practice (false advertising) and not repeat it; punitive damages may also be imposed.
qs.hint: Money back, medical bills, the false ad.
qs.ans: Refund, compensation, corrective advertisement, discontinue unfair practice

qs.q: “Principles of management are not as rigid as principles of pure science.” In the light of this statement, explain the nature of principles of management (any six features).
qs.model:
Management principles deal with human behaviour, so they are flexible guidelines, not exact laws. Their nature:

  1. Universal applicability: used in all types and sizes of organisations.
  2. General guidelines: guides to action, not readymade solutions.
  3. Formed by practice and experimentation: based on managers' experience and experiments.
  4. Flexible: can be modified to suit the situation.
  5. Mainly behavioural: aim to influence human behaviour.
  6. Cause and effect relationship: tell the likely result of an action; contingent: application depends on the situation.

qs.q: Identify and explain three limitations of planning highlighted in the case.
qs.passage: SkyCart, a drone-delivery start-up, spent eight months and ₹60 lakh on market studies and consultants before making its plan. By the time the plan was ready, a new rule restricted drone flights over residential areas, and two rivals had already launched. The founder, Ms. Tanya Gill, admitted, “Our plan was perfect on paper, but it gave us no guarantee.”

points.p: Explained + quote: ₹60 lakh on studies and consultants
Explained + quote: eight months; rivals launched first
May not work in a dynamic environment / does not guarantee success named
Explained + quote: a new rule restricted drone flights / “gave us no guarantee”

qs.model:
(i) Planning involves huge costs: research, experts and meetings cost a lot. SkyCart spent “₹60 lakh on market studies and consultants”.

(ii) Planning is time-consuming: it took “eight months”, by which time “two rivals had already launched”.

(iii) Planning may not work in a dynamic environment: the environment changes; “a new rule restricted drone flights”. Hence, as the founder says, planning does not guarantee success.
qs.hint: Money spent, months taken, a new rule, no guarantee.
qs.ans: Huge costs, time-consuming, may not work in a dynamic environment (does not guarantee success)

qs.q: Identify and explain three limitations of controlling highlighted in the case.
qs.passage: QuickBite fitted GPS trackers on its delivery bikes to control delivery times. Riders protested, saying they felt watched all the time. The system also cost ₹40 lakh, which the small company found hard to afford. Then a new city rule closed several roads at night, and delivery times rose, though managers could do nothing about it.

points.p: Explained + quote: riders protested about GPS
Explained + quote: ₹40 lakh hard to afford
Explained + quote: city rule closed roads; managers could do nothing

qs.model:
(i) Resistance from employees: employees feel restricted by control. Riders “protested, saying they felt watched all the time”.

(ii) Costly affair: control systems need heavy expenditure. The GPS system “cost ₹40 lakh, which the small company found hard to afford”.

(iii) Little control on external factors: government rules, technology and competition are outside the firm's control. “A new city rule closed several roads… managers could do nothing.”
qs.ans: Resistance from employees, costly affair, little control on external factors

qs.q: Explain any six factors affecting the capital structure of a company.

points.p: Regulatory framework / stock market conditions / floatation cost

qs.model:
(i) Cash flow position: strong cash flows support more debt.

(ii) Interest coverage ratio: higher ICR allows more debt.

(iii) Return on investment: high ROI favours trading on equity.

(iv) Tax rate: interest is deductible, so a high tax rate favours debt.

(v) Control: to retain control, debt is preferred to new equity.

(vi) Stock market conditions: in a boom, equity is easier to raise.
qs.hint: Cash flow, ICR, DSCR, ROI, cost of debt, tax, cost of equity, floatation, risk, flexibility, control, regulation, market.
